extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and educated readers of sociology/anthropology/comparative politics
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and synthesis of the conditions, processes, and traits by which small human groups aggregate into larger political societies; explains factors that further or hinder political integration across historical and ethnographic cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomadic instinct / mobility hinders aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence or absence of the nomadic instinct strongly influences the possibility of political integration: wandering habits, even when forced into agriculture, hinder aggregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kookies 'never occupying the same place for more than two or three years'; Mishmees 'never name their villages'; Bachassins (Litakun) twice removed in ten years. Conclusion: people little attached to localities are not easily united into large societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual traits enabling cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Social life presupposes intelligence that perceives and regulates the benefits of cooperation; unreflectiveness, deficient causal consciousness, and lack of constructive imagination hinder cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration/anti-pattern: Arab boatmen on the Nile chant while hauling but do not synchronize pulls — efforts lack unity of rhythm, producing ineffective combined action. Implication: early cooperation works only under peremptory command and requires intellectual faith in a commander (credulity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical, moral, and intellectual fitness for combined action
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration is prevented in many races by unfitnesses of nature — physical, moral, and intellectual — which impede political integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General principle referencing multiple passages: some peoples lack dispositions necessary for aggregation; these innate dispositions interact with environmental conditions to determine extent of integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likeness of kind / kinship (blood relationship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social union requires a considerable likeness of kind among united individuals; likeness is often insured initially by kinship in blood, which fosters cooperation and cohesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethnographic examples: Bushmen (families alone form associations), Rock Veddahs (small clans partition forest), New-Zealanders (Ngati = offspring). Humboldt: 'Savages know only their own family... a tribe appears to them but a more numerous assemblage of relations.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage systems' effect on cohesion (monogamy vs polygyny/polyandry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different marital systems produce different degrees and types of family connections; monogamy produces the most definite and wide‑spreading family ramifications and hence favors the largest, most coherent societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: polyandry produces children 'something less than half brothers and sisters'; polygyny produces many half-siblings; monogamy usually yields children all of same blood on both sides, strengthening kin-clusters and later gens/tribes and larger compound societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community of religion / common cult
rubrics_metrics.description: A community of religion — likeness of ideas and sentiments embodied in worship of a common deity — is an all-important bond that holds compound clusters together and checks antagonisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Origins: ancestor-worship arising from propitiation of deceased family founders. Historical examples: primitive Egyptian cities with special divinities, Greek family sacred rites, Roman curiae (sacrifice presiding), Hindu joint family assembling for common ancestor sacrifices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared language, traditions, and customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Community of language, traditions, ideas, and sentiments facilitates cooperation; differences in speech, thought, feeling, and custom hinder combined action by generating misunderstandings and alienation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/implication: quarrels even among speakers of same language; where a food or animal is sacred to one group and contemptible to another, cooperation is hindered. Grote's list for Hellenic bonds includes fellowship of language and like manners/dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint exposure to external forces / military cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Joint exposure to the same external actions and joint reactions against them (especially cooperation in war) are leading causes of social union and integration; war initiates unions that may become permanent political organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethnographic and historic examples: Karens uniting against common enemies; Hotentots allying against stronger nations; New Caledonian districts forming for protection; Israelites uniting in David's time; Greeks uniting against Xerxes; German tribes massing against Rome; England and France consolidating during wars. Initially unions often exist only for military purposes; internal administrations remain independent until habitual joint action consolidates cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survival advantage of societies with strong military cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the struggle among societies, 'the survival of the fittest' favors those with greater military cooperation; non-cooperating smaller communities are liable to be destroyed or absorbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fulbe advance where neighboring small tribes lack union; Damaras being piecemeal destroyed/enslaved when adjacent groups don't rise to defend; Inca conquests where provinces defended themselves without general opposition. This elimination process promotes the spread of varieties best adapted for social life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual compounding from small to large aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration necessarily begins with formation of simple small groups and advances by compounding these into larger bodies; larger aggregates require greater cohesion and organization to resist strains of increased size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical illustrations: primitive Egypt's nomes uniting into Upper/Lower Egypt then one; Greek villages to towns to states to inter-state unions; English principalities massing into Heptarchy then united whole. Analogy to physics: resistance to strain changes with scale, so only progressively more cohesive societies can form larger aggregates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints and coercion vary with stage of integration
rubrics_metrics.description: As social integration advances the aggregate exercises increasing restraints (coercive forces) over its units; coercion is slight at first, may become extreme at a stage, and afterward relaxes or changes form as societies industrialize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early motives: desire for protection prompts attachment to group; examples of coercive practices: seizure/enslavement of those apart from tribe (Patagonians, Chinooks). Later forms include registration systems, passports, slavery/serfdom; as industrial type develops coercion softens and is replaced by pecuniary interests and family bonds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decreasing personal mobility with integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance in integration is accompanied by decreasing ability of individuals to move between groups and to move place to place; members become less free to leave society or their locality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributing factors: settlement (vs nomadism), material interests, slavery, serfdom. Examples: ancient Mexicans and Peruvians punished for leaving provinces; Japanese registration requiring certificates to change residence; passport systems in despotic European states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitat and geography influence integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical environment — ability of habitat to support large population, facilities for intercourse within its area, and presence or absence of natural barriers — can favor or impede the growth and keeping together of large societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General guidance: such geographic conditions either enable cooperation and cohesion or hinder them by making internal communication and coercion difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of growth / incorporation (raiding to annexation)
rubrics_metrics.description: While small aggregates grow by petty incorporations (taking game, abducting women, adopting men), larger aggregates grow by enslaving conquered people and by annexation; as aggregations compound, desire to absorb adjacent societies increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence: petty raiding → enslavement → bodily annexation → formation of still larger aggregates. This pattern explains how political mass increases over stages of integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption and incorporation practices strengthen groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices of adoption (and related rites such as mock birth or exchange of blood) are modes by which societies increase numbers and strengthen themselves, analogous to earlier family-strengthening desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: North American tribes adopting captives (alternatively torture); Roman practice of adoption into families historically tied to tribal strengthening; analogous medieval practices (attachment to lords, burghs, guilds) when local integration incomplete.
